title: Microsoft’s Aion 1.0 Instruct: A better on-device language model for Windows
summary: Swapping the in-OS AI inference engine in Windows 11 is much like swapping out the tires of a car — while in the middle of a Grand Prix race. But Microsoft’s embedded Phi Silica small language model soon will be replaced by the company’s new Aion series of models , first through the Windows Insider program, followed by general availability across the Windows platform by the end of January 2027. That’s not long to run a transition, especially when there is third-party code written on top of the existing Windows AI framework that currently runs on Phi Silica. That’s on top of Windows’ own built-in AI-powered features that use Phi Silica to manage tooling like Click-To-Go and the Recall semantic memory. Replacing Phi Silica By the standards of AI model development Phi Silica is getting long in the tooth . Two years is an aeon in AI time, with the big frontier LLMs bringing out new releases two or three times a year. So, it’s not surprising that Microsoft has begun the process of replacing Phi with a model that is smaller and faster and has a significantly bigger context window. The replacement is Aion 1.0 Instruct , one of a new generation of Microsoft’s own AI labs models, unlike Phi Silica, which came directly from Microsoft Research. That’s an important distinction, as the Phi family of models was initially an experiment in using synthetic data in the form of textbooks to produce small language models. That approach proved to be particularly effective, and the new Aion small language model builds on that work but with the aim of delivering a model that works in the constrained environment of a desktop PC’s hardware. Aion isn’t the only new model from Microsoft; I recently looked at the company’s larger-scale frontier-class LLMs in the MAI family . These too offer PC-scaled Flash variants, though these do require more memory and compute than Aion, which is tuned for the 40 TOPS (trillions of operations per second) level of inference power delivered by NPUs from Qualc

title: Anthropic says it moved its Claude API from Python to Rust with no downtime
summary: When Anthropic decided to port its Messages API from Python to Rust, Claude wrote the code in about a week. But proving the new system worked as well as the old one, post-migration, was the real project. Anthropic engineers addressed this validation problem by turning the production Messages API itself into a verifier. It tested the new Rust version on production traffic, identified where it differed, and automatically sent out agents to fix those differences. The new Rust-based API now uses about 70% less CPU per request, 80% less memory, and cuts median time to first token by about 20%, a change achieved without ever taking the service offline or freezing feature development, the company said. The project revealed that it’s feasible to migrate production systems with Claude without taking an API offline or slowing development, Anthropic’s engineering team said in a new blog post . “Now that the hard part is no longer writing new code, we need to build sufficient confidence that the new system behaves like the old one,” they wrote. Verification is the bottleneck The Anthropic team launched the Messages API in 2023 as a simple Python “request forwarder.” It is the primary way both customers and its own internal apps reach Claude. But Claude has subsequently experienced monumental growth; from early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew by more than 1,800 times, according to the Anthropic engineers. As the model became more and more capable and further integrated with codebases, it also developed shared dependencies with Python libraries. By late 2025, every request had to be validated, converted into a prompt, tokenized, and screened by safety classifiers; tokens sent in reply had to be sorted into text, thinking, and tool calls. Python added overhead to each step. “Traffic eventually grew far beyond what the initial Python service was built for, and we quickly needed to find a way to make the service much more efficient,” the engineers explained. title: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite
summary: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025 . It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics. Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO . In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck. sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy! It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync: The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most. Update : Hah! Turns out I wrote about this application of sqlite_rsync back in October 2024 when the tool was first released. Tags: backups , sqlite
